No, they don't. A language model on its own won't remember what a student told your assistant last week.

**Example.** On Monday, Sam tells the assistant, "My project uses 3 mm acrylic." The next Monday, Sam asks, "What should I keep in mind when cutting my material?" If your program sends the model only that new question, the model has no way to know about the acrylic.

**General idea.** As you've already explained, a model knows what it learned in training plus the text it's given. Chatting with it doesn't add to that training. Model APIs (the way your code calls a model) are typically **stateless**: nothing from one request carries into the next [unless something stores it and supplies it again](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/llm-gateway/conversations).

It's an easy assumption to make, because some chat apps do seem to remember you. That memory comes from software around the model. Some model services can also [store conversation history for you](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state), but it's a feature you have to use, and the saved text still has to reach the model.

**For your design,** memory is a job your team has to build:

1. **Save** the useful facts, for example in a file or database, labeled by student.
2. **Look up** that student's facts when they come back.
3. **Include** them in the text you send the model.

You get to choose what's worth keeping. More text sent to the model generally means more cost, which matters on your budget.

**Your turn:** name one thing your assistant should save between visits and one it shouldn't bother saving, and say why. Context and memory is next on your path, so I can turn this into a short lesson when you're ready.

Sources: [AssemblyAI: conversations](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/llm-gateway/conversations) · [OpenAI: conversation state](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state)
